newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan tightlipped on resignation.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan tightlipped on resignation.

text.p: Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan kept Turkey on tenderhooks on Tuesday over reports that the end of his year-old tenure as the NATO member country's first Islamist leader was imminent.
Erbakan made no specific mention of a plan to hand over power to his pro-Western coalition partner Tansu Ciller in an hour-long speech to MPs of his Islam-based Welfare Party.

Members of the True Path Party government ally and the Turkish press say Erbakan will resign on Wednesday morning in a bid to swap jobs with Deputy Prime Minister Ciller and go to early elections before the end of the year.
"Welfare is working with all its might for democracy and human rights. If sacrifices are necesary, it will make them willingly," he said.
Anti-Islamist opposition from the influential army has forced Erbakan's coalition to the brink of collapse. Istanbul shares fell 1.07 percent in morning trading on political worries, brokers said.
A far-right leader with a key position in parliament said on Monday he would back government efforts to push the power transfer and election laws through the national assembly.
"There is a majority in parliament. No-one should have any worries about that," Erbakan said.

He assured the party faithful there was no going back from snap polls, which many analysts believe would give the Islamists a greater mandate. "We will have early elections as soon as possible to refuel in midair," he said. "The flight goes on."
Parliament must approve Erbakan's plans but defections from Ciller's wing have cost the ruling alliance its majority in the 550-seat chamber.
Support from rightist powerbroker Muhsin Yazicioglu's eight MPs would give the government 282 deputies on paper, enough to win approval if they can hold on to their own restive MPs.
But Erbakan cannot hand Ciller his duties without first giving his resignation to President Suleyman Demirel, a veteran politican who would direct the formation of a new government.
Demirel's office said there was so far no meeting planned between the prime minister and the president on Wednesday. "No such request (from Erbakan) has come to us yet," a spokesman told Reuters.
Military pressure has hindered Erbakan's goal of increasing the role of Islam in public life and building bridges to Turkey's Moslem neighbours.

The generals, who have staged three coups since 1960, say their fight with religious activism is a matter of "life or death" for Turkey, a secularist nation with ambitions of joining the European Union.

Erbakan presided at the weekend over the founding summit in Istanbul of the Developing-Eight (D-8) Moslem nations. But he has been helpless to stop growing military ties with Israel that have angered the Arabs.
Five Turkish navy vessels docked in an Israeli port on Monday in defiance of the prime minister's pro-Arab stance.

Israeli security sources said the flotilla comprised a submarine, three small warships and a supply vessel. Turkey, Israel and the United States agreed last month to hold joint naval manoeuvres in the eastern Mediterranean in the summer.

Turkey's security apparatus stepped up its campaign against Islamist activities at home. The state-run Anatolian news agency said undercover policemen had been ordered to monitor mosques and religious education courses for signs of Moslem militancy.

"From now on we will put more importance on intelligence work. Speeches that constitute crimes will be recorded by tape cassettes and cameras," the agency quoted an unnamed senior police official as saying.
